Where is Burlington, Vermont, and how is the city laid out?

Burlington sits on the eastern shore of Lake Champlain, about 45 miles south of the Canadian border, and is the county seat of Chittenden County. The city covers roughly 15.5 square miles, about a third of it water, and the land rises steeply from the lakeshore.

Settlement began in 1783, the town was organized in 1785, and the city was incorporated in 1865. The 2020 census counted 44,743 residents, which made Burlington the most populous municipality in Vermont.

Several distinct areas shape what a house here is like to sell:

  • Downtown, the commercial center around the Church Street Marketplace.
  • The Hill Section, described as the wealthiest neighborhood.
  • The Old North End, the oldest and most densely populated area.
  • The South End, a former industrial district now known for its arts scene.
  • The New North End, the most populous neighborhood.
  • The University District, near the University of Vermont and student housing.

A triple-decker in the Old North End and a single-family house in the New North End attract different buyers and carry different rules, so the first step in any sale is to name the type of property you own.

What drives the Burlington economy and housing demand?

Education, health care, trade, transportation and utilities anchor the Burlington economy. The largest employers are the University of Vermont Medical Center, with over 8,200 workers, and the University of Vermont, with about 4,125. Champlain College is also based in the city.

The median age in Burlington is 27.8, and the median household income for 2017 to 2021 was $59,331. Burlington Electric Department reports that about 60 percent of Burlington residents are renters, so rental property is a large part of the housing stock.

Owners of rental buildings should expect buyers to ask about rental registration, inspection history and energy compliance, covered in the sections below.

How do Burlington's climate and lakefront affect an older house?

Burlington has a humid continental climate with cold winters and warm, humid summers. Average annual precipitation is about 43 inches and average snowfall about 86 inches.

Snow, ice and long heating seasons put a premium on a few features, and buyers and inspectors tend to look at them first:

  • Roof condition and ice damming at the eaves.
  • Attic and basement insulation and air sealing.
  • Heating system age and fuel type.

Burlington Electric Department notes that many of the city's rental buildings were built decades ago without much attention to weatherization, and about 95 percent of rental buildings use natural gas for space heating. If you own an older house and do not want to manage repairs before listing, selling as-is for cash avoids the cost of fixing items a buyer's inspection might raise.

How do Burlington's roads, airport and transit connect it to the region?

Interstate 89 runs close to the city, and US Routes 2 and 7 pass through it. The Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport is owned by the city but located in neighboring South Burlington. Amtrak's Ethan Allen Express has served the city since 2022, connecting it to New York City, and Green Mountain Transit provides local bus service.

The public schools are run by the Burlington School District, which includes Burlington High School and two magnet programs.

How is Burlington property tax billed and how do you appeal a value?

Burlington property tax is paid in four quarterly installments due on the 12th of August, November, March and June. If the 12th falls on a weekend, payment is due the next business day. The city's fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30, and the Clerk/Treasurer's Office handles payments, interest and penalties.

The bill combines municipal tax and education tax. For the education portion, the Vermont Department of Taxes says a property with a filed Homestead Declaration (Form HS-122) and no business or rental use is billed at the homestead education rate, while a property that is not a primary residence is billed at the nonhomestead rate.

The Vermont Tax Department ordered a citywide reappraisal in 2018, with a valuation date of April 1, 2021 and new values taking effect for tax year 2022. The goal was to value every property at 100 percent of fair market value. An owner who thinks the current value is too high can grieve it:

StepWhat the city says
Appraisals take effectApril 1
Change of Assessment Notices mailedFirst week of May
Grievance deadline14 calendar days from the notice
Board of Assessors hearingsTypically third week of May
Appeal to Board of Tax Appeals14 days from the decision letter

The Board of Assessors says an owner must first present credible evidence that the value is too high, and that general statements of belief are not enough. The Assessor's Office is on the ground floor of City Hall at 149 Church Street.

What does Vermont's property transfer tax mean for a Burlington sale?

Vermont charges a property transfer tax on the transfer of title, and by statute the transferee, the buyer, is liable unless the parties agree otherwise. The governing law is 32 V.S.A. chapter 231, and a purchase contract can shift the cost, so read the contract line that covers it.

The Department of Taxes lists these rates, which include a 0.22 percent clean water surcharge:

  • A general rate of 1.25 percent, or 1.47 percent with the surcharge.
  • For a buyer's principal residence, 0.5 percent on the first $200,000, then 1.47 percent above that.
  • For year-round habitable property that is not the buyer's principal residence and is not a long-term rental, 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.
  • For principal residences financed in part through certain housing programs, the first $250,000 is exempt.

A property transfer return is delivered to the town clerk when the deed is delivered for recording, and the tax is due within 30 days of closing. Because rates depend on how the buyer will use the house, an investor buying a Burlington duplex faces a different calculation than a family buying to live in it.

What Burlington rules affect rental owners and vacant houses?

The Permitting and Inspections Department enforces Burlington's Minimum Housing Ordinance, which requires rentals to be registered. Registration is covered by Sec. 18-15 of the city code, and short-term and long-term rentals are registered through the city's online portal. The department also enforces a Vacant Building Ordinance (Chapter 8, Article 3) and handles building and zoning permits. Its office is at 645 Pine Street, phone 802-863-0442.

The Weatherization Ordinance adds a requirement for high energy use rental buildings. It applies where total space heating use is above 50,000 BTU per square foot per year, and it phased in by use level from January 1, 2022 to January 1, 2025. Owners must hire a BPI-certified contractor for an audit and then for the work, and the city says re-inspection fees and fines follow if work is not completed on time unless DPI grants an extension or waiver.

Burlington Electric states that the earlier Time of Sale Energy Efficiency Ordinance was effective through December 31, 2021, and points readers to the Minimum Housing Code Weatherization Ordinance, effective January 1, 2022. You can check a building's status in the city's property database, where a green bar means compliant and a yellow bar means not yet compliant.

If you own a rental that has not met these requirements, a cash buyer buying as-is may take on the compliance work, which can be easier than finishing it yourself before a sale.

Can a Burlington homeowner add an accessory dwelling unit before selling?

An accessory dwelling unit is a permitted use in Burlington where there is an owner-occupied single-family home. Section 5.4.5 of the city's zoning ordinance limits the unit to 900 square feet or 30 percent of the principal home's gross floor area, whichever is greater, and requires wastewater certification by the Department of Public Works.

Approval depends on owner occupancy. If neither unit is owner-occupied, the approval is void and the kitchen in the accessory unit must be removed within 90 days. A deed reference to the ADU permit must also be recorded before the certificate of occupancy is issued.

That owner-occupancy rule is worth knowing before you sell. A buyer who plans to rent both units may not be able to keep an ADU that was approved on owner occupancy, so ask the Planning and Zoning office how the rule applies before you advertise the unit as income.

More questions about Burlington, VT

How often is property tax due in Burlington, VT?

Four times a year. Installments are due on the 12th of August, November, March and June, or the next business day if the 12th falls on a weekend.

Who pays the Vermont property transfer tax?

The buyer, unless the parties agree otherwise. State law makes the tax the liability of the transferee of the title.

How long do I have to grieve my Burlington assessment?

14 calendar days from the date on the Change of Appraisal Notice. Hearings before the Board of Assessors are typically held in the third week of May.

Do Burlington rental owners need to register their rentals?

Yes. The Minimum Housing Ordinance requires registration under Sec. 18-15 of the city code, and the Permitting and Inspections Department runs the process.

What is the Burlington weatherization ordinance?

It requires high energy use rental buildings, those above 50,000 BTU per square foot per year, to complete an audit and weatherization work by a staged deadline between 2022 and 2025.
